sentences.text: This medium-sized carnivorous predator reached an estimated body length of 3 to 4 meters.
Its body proportions were generally similar to other primitive pliosaurids, such as the well-preserved Peloneustes.
The animal possesses two unique traits: a palpebral projection at the midheight of the eye socket margin and a distinct trapezoidal posteroventral coracoid process.
It is distinguished by a combination of rare traits including narrow neural spines, a back-directed retroarticular projection, a hill on the coronoid depression, and specific rib facet placements.
A bone projection midway along the front margin of the eye orbit and a trapezoid-shaped coracoid process are features not seen in other plesiosaurs.
Evidence suggests it hunted in the upper pelagic zone using a slender elongated jaw and small curved teeth with finely serrated edges.
The genus is known solely from the holotype specimen MPPL 18797, which is housed at the Museo Paleontologico e della Preistoria 'P. Leonardi' in Ferrara.
The remains were collected during the 1980s from the Kaberlaba quarry in the Asiago Municipality of the Vicenza Province in northern Italy.
Although discovered in the 1980s, the specimen was not thoroughly described until 2014 by Andrea Cau and Federico Fanti.
The genus was named in 2015 by Cau and Fanti, with the type species designated as Anguanax zignoi, though some records state the naming occurred in 2016.
Anguanax lived during the Late Jurassic period in rocks of the Rosso Ammonitico Veronese Formation in northern Italy.
The fossils date to the middle Oxfordian stage of the early Late Jurassic, approximately 160 million years ago, or the Callovian to Oxfordian stages, approximately 165.3 to 159 million years ago.
Originally described as exclusively plesiosaurian by Zigno, the remains were later found to include crocodylomorph elements, though neither group could be identified to the family level.
